cardInfo.summary: A script that runs on its own: the script an automation runs, when, which outside services the script may call, and what each run may use. A realm administrator turns the automation on and pays for the automation's runs.

attributes.readMe:
## Automation

Runs a Realm Runner script with nobody watching: on a schedule, once at a set time, or when another service sends a webhook. The card says which script runs, when, which outside services the script may call, and what each run and each month may use.

![The isolated view: state, payer, next and last run, the script and each trigger in words](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6852fe2d49f41a717efaebc17ed2d892861dcee8/automation/Spec/images/isolated.png)

```ts
import { Automation } from '@cardstack/catalog/automation/automation';
@field automation = linksTo(Automation);
```

Create an Automation in the workspace the script works on, link the script, then add the triggers, outside services and limits. A type that extends `Automation` is an automation too.

### Who turns it on, and who pays

* A new automation runs nothing. A realm administrator turns the automation on, and that person pays for every run. Each run acts as that person, within the card's limits.
* Editing the card never changes who pays. Raising a limit, or turning on batched AI, pauses the automation until someone turns the automation on again.
* Only a realm administrator can change an automation. Sharing rules that let others edit some cards never reach an automation.

### Turning an automation on

A realm administrator presses **Turn on the automation** in the isolated view's Status section. The switch-on screen shows:

* **The estimate**: the most one run can cost under the per-run limits, times the runs the triggers make in an average month, plus each one-time run still to come. The screen also shows what the person's last Preview cost. Boxel charges a Preview to whoever runs the Preview, so the estimate leaves Previews out.
* **What the estimate leaves out**: the indexing that each run's saves cause, the daily storage of the files the runs create, and runs that a webhook delivery starts, since no schedule predicts webhook deliveries. Boxel counts these charges toward the monthly limit too.
* **The monthly limit**, filled in from the card. Boxel turns an automation on only with a monthly limit, and the monthly limit can't be below the daily limit. A person who enters another limit changes the card's monthly limit, and Boxel turns the automation on at that limit.
* **Becoming the payer**: Boxel charges every scheduled run to the person who turns the automation on, and the storage of the files the runs create for every day the automation’s status reads On. The monthly limit stops Boxel from starting runs, and Boxel stops charging for storage while the automation is paused, waiting for credits, waiting for key approval or done. Any realm administrator can pause the automation, or resume the automation and become the payer instead.
* **The keys the automation uses**: each outside service the card declares, with the key approval the service needs. Boxel asks for every approval when a realm administrator turns the automation on, never at the first run, and the automation runs nothing until every approval is in place.

When someone raises a limit above what the payer agreed to, or turns on batched AI, Boxel pauses the automation. The Status section then offers **Review and resume**, which opens the same screen. Whoever resumes the automation agrees to the card as the card stands and becomes the payer.

### Key approval at switch-on

An automation that calls an outside service with a key needs the key's owner to approve the automation's use of the key. The switch-on screen shows each service as approved, or names who approves the service:

* **The payer's own keys**, and keys the payer shares with the realm: the payer approves in the same step. Pressing **Turn on the automation and pay** turns the automation on and opens Boxel's secure window, where the payer approves every call the automation makes with the payer's keys in one confirmation. If the browser blocks the secure window, the screen offers **Open the secure window**. Boxel never shows a key's value outside the secure window. Once the approval lands, the screen shows the automation as on.
* **A key another person shares with the realm**: the screen names the key and the key's owner. Boxel names a person only to someone who already works with that person in a realm, and says "the owner of the key" otherwise. The automation turns on waiting for key approval and runs nothing until the key's owner approves.
* **A suspended share**: the share's owner resumes the share before anyone approves the call, and the automation waits until then.
* **No key shared yet**: the service needs a key that a realm administrator shares with the realm first, so the screen can't turn the automation on yet. In place of **Turn on the automation and pay**, the screen offers **Share a key**, which opens the secure window's share page for the realm. When the person comes back, the screen reads the key approvals again.

An approval lasts while the automation stays as approved. An edit to the automation's script, triggers, params or outside services, or a higher limit on outside calls, makes the automation wait until each key's owner approves again, and an edit back to the approved automation needs no new approval. Other edits to the limits keep the approvals. Whoever resumes a paused automation becomes the payer, and the new payer approves the new payer's own keys.

### What the card holds

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `script` | A JavaScript file in the same workspace, run as a Realm Runner script: the body of an async function with the `realm` object. The edit view edits and saves the file in place. |
| `triggers` | **Schedule**: a cron expression (or a macro such as `@daily`) in a time zone, at most once every 5 minutes, with an optional stop after a number of runs or after a date. **Once**: a date and a time in a time zone. **Webhook**: one of the workspace's incoming webhooks. Each trigger has a label, unique within the automation, that keeps the trigger's count of runs. |
| `operations` | The only outside calls the script may make: a card type and one of the type's `callApi` operations. |
| `caps` | For each run: outside calls, data received, saves, AI requests, AI spending in credits and run time (up to 20 minutes). For each day and each month: the credits all runs together may spend. A run stops at the first limit the run reaches. |
| `params` | Values the script reads as `realm.current.automation.params`. |
| `batchedAI`, `batchDeadlineMinutes` | AI requests at about half the price, answered later. The deadline is how long a run waits for the answers, up to 1,440 minutes and an hour when empty; Boxel asks again at full price for any answer not back by then. |

Whether an automation is on, who pays, the next run and the run counts live on the server, not on the card.

### Run milestones and tasks

A script names its milestones up front, marks each one as the script reaches it, and reports the notable tasks inside each one. The card reads the milestones and tasks from the runs, never from a field.

```js
realm.progress.plan(['Fetch open issues', 'Group by label', 'Write digest']);
realm.progress.milestone('Fetch open issues');
// …
realm.progress.task(`Fetched ${issues.length} open issues`);
realm.progress.task(`Skipped ${pullRequests} pull requests`);
realm.progress.milestone('Group by label');
```

* `realm.progress.plan([...names])` declares 1 to 50 names, in order. Write the plan as a list of names: the card reads the plan from the script's text to show the milestones ahead before any run.
* `realm.progress.milestone(name)` starts that milestone and ends the one before. A name the plan doesn't list still counts, and shows as not in the plan.
* `realm.progress.task(text)` reports a notable task inside the current milestone, in up to 200 characters of plain words that name what the task acted on, such as *Grouped the bug label*. Report a task a person would check, not one per item of a loop: a run records at most 200 milestones and 200 tasks, and 5,000 progress and console calls. A task before the first milestone throws.
* `realm.progress.count(done, total)` records nothing. A run that calls the method says once in the run's log to report tasks instead.
* None of the four needs `await`. A bad argument throws in the script.

### What each format shows

Only realm administrators see the state, the payer, the runs and a run's milestones. The card names the payer only to an editor who shares a workspace with the payer. Anyone else sees the card's own fields and the milestones the script declares. A prerendered view reads neither the status nor the script, so it shows the card's own fields alone.

* **Isolated**: everything on the card, with the state and the reason for a pause, the payer, the next and last run, each trigger's runs and runs left, and each milestone of the run in progress or the last run, with its time and the tasks the script reported inside the milestone. A milestone with more than 5 tasks lists the latest 5, and a button shows or hides the earlier ones. The **Runs** section lists every run, with a running run's milestone and latest task, and updates as the script reports tasks.
* **Embedded**: the title and state, every trigger in words, the next and last run, and the milestones. A narrow row shows the milestones as a bar under where the run stands, such as *Failed in Match invoices*. A row 36rem wide or more shows each milestone on a track with its time, for runs of up to 8 milestones.

![The embedded view of a run in progress, with each milestone on a track](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6852fe2d49f41a717efaebc17ed2d892861dcee8/automation/Spec/images/embedded.png)

* **Fitted**: each size adds the next most useful fact. A badge or strip shows the title and, from 240px wide, the state. Then the first trigger, or where a running or failed run stands. Then the milestones as a bar. A tile adds the last run and any warning (*No script yet*, *Batched AI*). A card, or a tile from 240px tall, adds the other triggers and the next run. A card, or a tile from 240px wide and 270px tall, lists the milestones around the current one, with how many come before and after, and with room for two lines a milestone, each milestone's time and latest task.

![The fitted view as a strip, a tile, a large tile and a card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6852fe2d49f41a717efaebc17ed2d892861dcee8/automation/Spec/images/fitted.png)

### The linked examples

Neither example is turned on.

* `Automation/weekly-card-count` counts the workspace's cards by type every Monday at 7:00 AM Chicago time, and whenever its webhook is called, into `reports/card-count.md`. A search answers 50 cards a page unless `page.size` asks for up to 100, so the script reads 100 cards at a time, asking for the next `page.number` until `truncated` is false. Two milestones, with one task each: how many cards of how many types the script counted, and the file the script wrote.
* `Automation/open-issues-digest` reads the open issues of the GitHub repository card `examples/GitHubRepository/boxel` every weekday morning, twice a day on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and once at a kick-off, and groups them by label into `reports/open-issues.md`. Its one outside call is the repository type's `openIssues`, made with the GitHub key of whoever turns the automation on. Three milestones, with tasks for the issues fetched, the pull requests skipped, the labels grouped and the digest written.

### Non-goals

* **Not a way to run any code.** An automation runs a Realm Runner script, never a card's command or a module the card names.
* **Not a way around the workspace's permissions.** A run acts as the person who turned the automation on, reaches outside the workspace only through its declared outside calls and AI requests, and its saves land together when the run finishes, or not at all.
